title: Blockchains create net new markets
gist: a16z's Robbie Peterson argues blockchains are the first technology to let the supply of markets catch up with latent demand, by making issuance permissionless and distribution global. His evidence is onchain RWA perps reaching a $1.4T run-rate in July (half of Hyperliquid's book) and onchain venues pricing WTI and pre-IPO stocks when traditional venues were closed or unavailable. He predicts new markets in compute, CPI and other oraclable risks, with value accruing to market issuers and venues.

themes.theme: Market supply, not demand, was the historical bottleneck

insights.claim: For most of financial history the scarce thing was the supply of new markets rather than demand for them; blockchains remove that bottleneck, which the author expects to trigger an explosion of net new markets.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Frames crypto's value as market-creation capacity, so value accrues to issuers and venues of new markets rather than to any single asset.
insights.quote: For most of financial history, the supply of new markets — not demand — was the bottleneck.

insights.claim: Markets are mechanisms for transferring risk, and any risk can be described on two independent axes: the unit (the underlying exposure) and the instrument (the mechanism that transfers it, such as spot, futures, perps, options or event contracts).
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: A usable taxonomy: new markets arise from a new unit, a new instrument, or a recombination of the two, which makes it easy to screen for gaps.
insights.quote: Markets are mechanisms for transferring risk.
insights.locator: Markets are mechanisms for transferring risk

insights.claim: Financial innovation has historically moved one axis at a time and slowly: grain spot markets predated Chicago grain futures (1865) by thousands of years, currencies floated in 1971 and got futures in 1972, listed equity options arrived in 1973, and ETFs only in 1993.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: The multi-decade lag between a demand and its tradable instrument is the gap onchain issuance is claimed to close.
insights.quote: Spot grain markets existed for thousands of years before Chicago listed grain futures in 1865.

insights.claim: New units of risk have been even rarer than new instruments: interest rates became widely tradeable in 1981, default risk via credit default swaps in 1994, volatility via VIX derivatives in 2004, and event outcomes only in the last few years through prediction markets.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Each new unit of risk spawned a large market, so the next new units (compute, macro indicators) could be similarly large.
insights.quote: Interest rates only became widely tradeable in 1981.
insights.locator: New units of risk have been even rarer

insights.claim: Latent demand preceded the markets that served it: farmers wanted to hedge harvests long before the CBOT and creditors wanted to offload default risk long before CDS, so growth was throttled by supply constraints (listing committees and legal frameworks, and geographic fragmentation).
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: If the constraint was supply-side gatekeeping, removing it should release pent-up volume in categories nobody has yet built.
insights.quote: Demand for these markets was arguably never the issue.

insights.claim: Because blockchains make issuance permissionless and distribution global, they remove both historical throttles on market supply; the author calls this the killer use case of crypto in its most distilled form.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Recasts crypto's core value proposition from money or assets to market formation, which shifts how to value protocols.
insights.quote: Blockchains are the first technology that lets the supply of markets catch up with latent global demand.

themes.theme: Crypto's category winners as net new units or instruments

insights.claim: Almost every category-defining crypto outcome (perps, spot DEXs, prediction markets, lending markets, memecoins, NFTs, tokenized physicals) is downstream of creating a net new market, and value has accrued to those who own issuance and/or exchange of these onchain markets.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: A single lens to explain past winners and to screen for future ones: who controls issuance or the venue for a new market.
insights.quote: From perps and spot DEXs to prediction markets to lending markets to memecoins, NFTs, and tokenized physicals
insights.locator: This thesis manifests empirically as well

insights.claim: On the unit side, crypto has made previously inexpressible exposures tradeable: events (an election, a Fed decision, a court ruling), individual credit relationships priced continuously via peer-to-peer lending, pre-IPO exposure formerly gated to secondary brokers, and even attention and cultural relevance via memecoins and NFTs.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Reframes memecoins and NFTs as crude but real markets in attention, rather than mere speculation.
insights.quote: On the unit side, crypto has engineered risk exposures that had little or no prior financial expression.

insights.claim: On the instrument side, crypto scaled novel transfer mechanisms: AMMs let a market exist before a market maker agreed to quote it, perps (proposed in 1993) collapsed fragmented dated exposure into one funding-rate-balanced contract, binary contracts turned events into $1-or-nothing markets, peer-to-pool lending replaced bilateral loans with a utilization curve, and bonding curves fused issuance with price discovery.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Each mechanism removes a dependency (market maker, dated expiry, counterparty, listing), which is where new markets come from.
insights.quote: AMMs let a market exist before a market maker agreed to quote it.

insights.claim: Permissionless issuance produces a lot of noise, which is the cost of removing the listing filter; the claim is not that every new market is good but that the market itself, not a committee, becomes the mechanism selecting which survive.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Concedes the main bear case (junk markets) and argues selection by liquidity is superior to gatekeeping, so expect heavy failure rates among new listings.
insights.quote: Permissionless issuance also produces a lot of noise.

themes.theme: Perps and Hyperliquid as proof of the thesis

insights.claim: Because perps are synthetic, the listing constraint collapses to a robust oracle and two counterparties willing to take opposite sides, so a leveraged market can exist for almost anything.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Oracle quality and counterparty depth are the true bottlenecks for new markets, which makes oracle providers and market makers key chokepoints.
insights.quote: the listing constraint collapses to two things: a robust oracle and two counterparties willing to take the other side

insights.claim: Hyperliquid is described as the closest thing to a global platform for financial coordination; HIP-3 and HIP-4 let users launch their own derivatives on the venue's global front end and monetize, so lower launch friction yields more markets with demand selecting winners.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Positions Hyperliquid as a market-creation platform whose moat is distribution plus permissionless listing, not just a perp exchange.
insights.quote: By this same logic, Hyperliquid is the closest thing we have to a global platform for financial coordination.

insights.claim: In July, onchain RWA perps volume reached a $1.4T run-rate and made up half of Hyperliquid's book, which the author reads as existing units of risk (equities, oil, memory stocks) meeting a new instrument and driving an explosion in volume.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Non-crypto underlyings now account for half of the leading perp venue's volume, so its growth is increasingly linked to traditional asset volatility.
insights.quote: In July, onchain RWA perps volume reached a $1.4T run-rate
insights.locator: Note too that some net new market

insights.claim: The dominant onchain market rotates each period to whatever the world wants to trade: US equities and commodities in Q4 2025, oil, gas and metals in H1 2026, and most recently semis and memory stocks.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Volume leadership follows macro and thematic attention within weeks, so onchain perp volume works as a live gauge of where speculative interest is moving.
insights.quote: In Q4 2025 it was US equities and commodities; in H1 2026 it was oil, gas, and metals, and most recently semis and memory stocks.
insights.locator: Note too that some net new market

themes.theme: Onchain price discovery wedge against traditional markets

insights.claim: Permissionless, 24/7 trading is becoming a wedge for price discovery to occur canonically onchain: during the February oil shock, with CME closed, WTI found price discovery on trade.xyz as one of the most liquid markets globally.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: If weekend and overnight shocks are priced onchain first, traditional venues may open by following onchain prices, which shifts who sets the reference price.
insights.quote: During the oil shock in February of this year, while CME was closed, WTI found price discovery on trade.xyz as one of the most liquid markets globally.

insights.claim: Pre-IPO perp markets for Cerebras and SpaceX priced the IPOs more accurately than bankers did, with only a marginal gap between the final-hour pre-IPO perp price and the actual market open price.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Suggests pre-IPO perps can serve as an open-market alternative to bookbuilding, which would threaten underwriter pricing power and IPO-pop economics.
insights.quote: pricing the IPOs more accurately than bankers
insights.locator: Similarly, we saw pre-IPO equities markets

insights.claim: Lack of 24/7 trading, geographic gating, lack of pre-IPO access and siloed margin are structural constraints of traditional markets that the author argues are a sustainable wedge for onchain markets.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Lists specific, testable incumbent weaknesses; watch whether CME, exchanges and brokers extend hours or cross-margining in response.

themes.theme: Forecast: what new markets come next and who captures value

insights.claim: The addressable universe of onchain markets is not today's set of assets but any risk that anyone, or any agent, anywhere wants to trade, because geography, listing committees and legal frameworks no longer constrain supply.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Expands the crypto TAM from assets to all tradeable risk, and the explicit mention of agents implies machine-driven market participation.
insights.quote: The addressable universe of onchain markets is not the set of assets that exist today

insights.claim: The author predicts continued growth in new ways to transfer old risk (commodities and FX perps, indices, 24/7 equity exposure) and in new units of risk (compute futures, perps on macro indicators like CPI, music, social trends, sports, and anything oraclable and two-sided).
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Names concrete product categories to watch for, notably compute and CPI perps, which would tie crypto venues to AI infrastructure and macro data.
insights.quote: compute futures, perps on macro indicators like CPI, music, social trends, sports

insights.claim: Value will be captured by the applications and protocols that issue new markets and by the venues that exchange them.
insights.speaker: Robbie Peterson
insights.so_what: Directs attention to issuance platforms and exchange venues, such as Hyperliquid, over holding the underlying assets.
insights.quote: The applications and protocols that issue those markets, and the venues that exchange them, are the ones that will capture the value.
